system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Immune-mediated central nervous system demyelination produces neurologic deficits separated in time and space, often including optic neuritis, sensory symptoms, and upper motor neuron findings.
vignette: A 29-year-old woman has painful loss of vision in one eye that improves over several weeks. Eight months later she develops numbness of the left leg and urinary urgency. Examination shows hyperreflexia in the left leg.
lead: Which diagnosis best explains this pattern?
distractor_notes: Guillain-Barré syndrome is a peripheral demyelinating neuropathy that usually causes symmetric ascending weakness and areflexia rather than episodic CNS deficits.
Myasthenia gravis causes fatigable neuromuscular-junction weakness without sensory loss, hyperreflexia, or optic neuritis.
Parkinson disease causes bradykinesia, rigidity, tremor, and postural instability rather than relapsing multifocal CNS deficits.
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis causes progressive motor neuron loss without sensory deficits or optic neuritis.
key_expl: Neurologic episodes involving different CNS locations at different times, including optic neuritis and upper motor neuron signs, are characteristic of multiple sclerosis.
objective: Recognize multiple sclerosis from dissemination of central nervous system deficits in time and space.
clues: optic neuritis followed months later by new neurologic deficits
hyperreflexia with sensory and bladder symptoms

sources.title: Multiple sclerosis
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes multiple sclerosis as an immune-mediated CNS disorder that damages myelin and causes varied neurologic symptoms that may relapse.

sources.title: Multiple Sclerosis
sources.support: NINDS describes multiple sclerosis as immune-mediated damage to myelin in the brain and spinal cord with episodic neurologic deficits.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta reduces striatal dopamine, decreasing direct-pathway activity and increasing indirect-pathway influence on movement.
vignette: A 68-year-old man has progressive bradykinesia, resting tremor, rigidity, and reduced arm swing while walking.
lead: Loss of neurons in which structure most directly causes this disorder?
distractors: Anterior horn of the spinal cord
distractor_notes: Lesions of the subthalamic nucleus classically cause hemiballismus rather than parkinsonism.
The caudate is prominently affected in Huntington disease, whereas Parkinson disease centers on nigrostriatal dopaminergic loss.
Cerebellar vermis disease produces truncal ataxia rather than bradykinesia and resting tremor.
Anterior horn cell degeneration causes lower motor neuron weakness, not the extrapyramidal syndrome shown.
key_expl: Parkinson disease is characterized by degeneration of dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta and reduced nigrostriatal dopamine.
objective: Link parkinsonian motor findings to loss of substantia nigra pars compacta dopaminergic neurons.

sources.title: Parkinson's disease
sources.support: MedlinePlus explains that Parkinson disease involves loss of brain cells that produce dopamine and causes tremor, rigidity, and slowed movement.

sources.title: Parkinson's Disease
sources.support: NINDS describes degeneration of dopamine-producing neurons, especially in the substantia nigra, as central to Parkinson disease.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Expansion of a CAG trinucleotide repeat in HTT produces a toxic polyglutamine-expanded huntingtin protein and autosomal dominant neurodegeneration with anticipation.
vignette: A 38-year-old man develops progressive chorea, irritability, and impaired executive function. His father developed similar symptoms at age 52.
lead: Which genetic change best explains the earlier onset in this patient?
correct: Expansion of a CAG repeat in HTT
distractors: Expansion of a CGG repeat in FMR1
Expansion of a CTG repeat in DMPK
distractor_notes: FMR1 CGG-repeat expansion causes fragile X syndrome, not Huntington disease.
DMPK CTG-repeat expansion causes myotonic dystrophy type 1.
SMN1 loss causes spinal muscular atrophy.
PMP22 duplication commonly causes Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1A.
key_expl: Huntington disease is caused by CAG-repeat expansion in HTT; larger expansions may be associated with earlier onset in successive generations.
objective: Recognize trinucleotide-repeat anticipation in Huntington disease as expansion of the HTT CAG repeat.

sources.title: Huntington's disease
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes Huntington disease as an autosomal dominant HTT CAG-repeat expansion disorder with anticipation.

sources.title: HTT gene
sources.support: The HTT gene contains a CAG repeat; expansion beyond the normal range causes Huntington disease.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Autoantibodies most often target postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, reducing functional receptor density and producing fatigable skeletal-muscle weakness.
vignette: A 31-year-old woman has ptosis and diplopia that worsen late in the day and improve after rest. Sensation and reflexes are normal.
lead: The most common antibodies in this disorder target which structure?
distractors: Muscarinic acetylcholine receptors in smooth muscle
Voltage-gated sodium channels at nodes of Ranvier
Dopamine D2 receptors in the striatum
distractor_notes: Presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channel antibodies are characteristic of Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome.
Muscarinic receptor dysfunction would affect autonomic target organs rather than produce isolated fatigable skeletal-muscle weakness.
Nodal sodium-channel dysfunction causes peripheral nerve conduction abnormalities, not the classic postsynaptic neuromuscular-junction pattern.
Striatal dopamine receptor abnormalities are not the cause of myasthenia gravis.
key_expl: Most myasthenia gravis is caused by antibodies against postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction.
objective: Connect fatigable ocular and bulbar weakness with antibody-mediated loss of postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors.

sources.title: Myasthenia gravis
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes myasthenia gravis as an autoimmune neuromuscular-junction disorder often involving acetylcholine receptor antibodies.

sources.title: Myasthenia Gravis
sources.support: NINDS explains that antibodies interfere with communication at the neuromuscular junction, commonly by targeting acetylcholine receptors.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Botulinum neurotoxin blocks presynaptic acetylcholine release at peripheral cholinergic synapses, producing cranial neuropathies followed by symmetric descending flaccid paralysis.
vignette: A 44-year-old man develops diplopia, dysphagia, dry mouth, and progressive descending weakness 18 hours after eating home-canned vegetables. He is afebrile and sensation is intact.
distractor_notes: Guillain-Barré syndrome usually produces ascending weakness and areflexia rather than cranial symptoms followed by descending paralysis after canned food.
Myasthenia gravis causes fatigable weakness but does not explain the acute autonomic symptoms and food exposure.
Tetanus produces painful rigidity and spasms from loss of inhibitory neurotransmission, not descending flaccid paralysis.
Organophosphate poisoning causes cholinergic excess with salivation, lacrimation, diarrhea, miosis, and bronchorrhea rather than dry mouth.
key_expl: Acute cranial neuropathies, autonomic symptoms, and descending flaccid paralysis after home-canned food are classic for foodborne botulism.
objective: Recognize foodborne botulism from cranial nerve dysfunction and descending paralysis after ingestion of improperly preserved food.
clues: descending weakness with dry mouth and diplopia

sources.title: Clinical Overview of Botulism
sources.support: CDC describes foodborne botulism as causing cranial nerve palsies and symmetric descending flaccid paralysis after ingestion of preformed toxin.

sources.title: Botulism
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes botulism as a toxin-mediated neurologic illness that can follow home-canned foods and cause double vision, swallowing difficulty, and paralysis.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Acute immune-mediated peripheral nerve injury, often after infection, causes rapidly progressive symmetric weakness with hyporeflexia or areflexia and can impair respiratory muscles.
vignette: A 35-year-old man develops tingling in his feet followed over 3 days by symmetric ascending leg weakness. Two weeks earlier he had a diarrheal illness. Deep-tendon reflexes are absent.
lead: Which diagnosis best explains these findings?
distractor_notes: Multiple sclerosis is a central demyelinating disorder and usually produces upper motor neuron signs such as hyperreflexia rather than areflexia.
Myasthenia gravis causes fatigable weakness without sensory paresthesias or loss of reflexes.
Botulism more often begins with cranial nerve symptoms and descending paralysis.
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is chronically progressive and combines upper and lower motor neuron signs without sensory symptoms.
key_expl: Acute ascending symmetric weakness and areflexia after a gastrointestinal infection are classic for Guillain-Barré syndrome.
objective: Diagnose Guillain-Barré syndrome from postinfectious ascending weakness and areflexia.

sources.title: Guillain-Barré syndrome
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes Guillain-Barré syndrome as an acute peripheral nerve disorder that can follow infection and cause weakness, tingling, and loss of reflexes.

sources.title: Guillain-Barré Syndrome
sources.support: NINDS describes rapidly progressive weakness and areflexia due to immune attack on peripheral nerves.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Alzheimer disease features extracellular beta-amyloid plaques and intracellular hyperphosphorylated tau neurofibrillary tangles with progressive synaptic and neuronal loss.
vignette: A 74-year-old woman has gradually progressive impairment of episodic memory followed by difficulty with language and navigation over 5 years.
lead: Which pathologic finding is most characteristic of this disorder?
correct: Extracellular beta-amyloid plaques with intracellular tau tangles
distractors: Loss of anterior horn cells with Bunina bodies
Lewy bodies confined to the substantia nigra without cortical disease
Spongiform change caused by bacterial toxin
distractor_notes: Anterior horn cell loss with Bunina bodies is associated with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
Peripheral demyelination is characteristic of disorders such as Guillain-Barré syndrome and does not explain progressive dementia.
Lewy bodies in the substantia nigra are associated with Parkinson disease; Alzheimer disease is defined by amyloid plaques and tau tangles.
Prion diseases can produce spongiform change, but they are not caused by bacterial toxin and typically progress much more rapidly.
key_expl: The core neuropathology of Alzheimer disease includes beta-amyloid plaques and hyperphosphorylated tau neurofibrillary tangles.
objective: Associate progressive Alzheimer-type dementia with beta-amyloid plaque deposition and tau neurofibrillary tangles.

sources.title: What Happens to the Brain in Alzheimer's Disease?
sources.support: NIA describes beta-amyloid plaques and abnormal tau tangles as key brain changes in Alzheimer disease.

sources.title: Alzheimer's disease
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes Alzheimer disease as a progressive brain disorder causing memory and cognitive decline.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Focal seizures arise from abnormal synchronized neuronal activity in a localized cortical network; temporal lobe seizures can produce stereotyped experiential auras and impaired awareness.
vignette: A 26-year-old man has recurrent episodes beginning with an intense sense of déjà vu followed by lip smacking and 1 minute of impaired awareness. He is confused for several minutes afterward.
lead: Where is the seizure focus most likely located?
distractor_notes: Primary motor cortex seizures more often cause focal clonic motor activity in the corresponding body region.
Occipital seizures commonly produce visual phenomena rather than déjà vu and automatisms.
The cerebellum coordinates movement but is not a typical origin of epileptic cortical seizures.
Spinal anterior horn neurons are lower motor neurons and do not generate focal impaired-awareness seizures.
key_expl: Déjà vu, automatisms such as lip smacking, impaired awareness, and postictal confusion are classic features of temporal lobe focal seizures.
objective: Localize focal impaired-awareness seizures with experiential aura and automatisms to the temporal lobe.
clues: lip smacking with impaired awareness and postictal confusion

sources.title: Epilepsy and Seizures
sources.support: NINDS describes focal seizures as arising in one part of the brain and causing localized sensory, experiential, motor, or awareness changes.

sources.title: Epilepsy
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes focal seizures and the possibility of impaired awareness, unusual sensations, and repetitive movements.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Reduced aqueous humor outflow through the trabecular meshwork chronically elevates intraocular pressure and damages retinal ganglion-cell axons at the optic nerve head.
vignette: A 63-year-old man has gradually progressive peripheral visual-field loss. Examination shows elevated intraocular pressure and optic-disc cupping. The anterior chamber angle is open.
lead: Which pathophysiologic abnormality most directly causes this disorder?
correct: Reduced aqueous humor drainage through the trabecular meshwork
distractors: Sudden pupillary blockage of the iridocorneal angle
distractor_notes: Sudden angle closure produces an acutely painful red eye with a closed angle rather than chronic open-angle disease.
Retinal artery occlusion causes sudden painless monocular vision loss, not gradual peripheral-field loss and cupping.
Lens-protein denaturation causes cataract and impaired visual clarity rather than elevated intraocular pressure.
Optic neuritis from demyelination causes painful visual loss and does not typically produce chronic pressure elevation and cupping.
key_expl: Primary open-angle glaucoma reflects impaired aqueous outflow through the trabecular meshwork, causing chronic intraocular-pressure-related optic nerve damage.
objective: Relate chronic open-angle glaucoma to impaired trabecular aqueous humor outflow and optic nerve cupping.
clues: open angle with elevated intraocular pressure and cupping

sources.title: Glaucoma
sources.support: NEI describes open-angle glaucoma as optic nerve damage often associated with impaired drainage and increased eye pressure.

sources.title: Glaucoma
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes glaucoma as optic nerve damage related to elevated eye pressure and distinguishes open-angle from angle-closure disease.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Separation of the neurosensory retina from the underlying retinal pigment epithelium causes photopsias, new floaters, and a curtain-like visual-field defect.
vignette: A 58-year-old highly myopic man suddenly notices flashes of light and many new floaters in his right eye, followed by a dark curtain descending across part of his visual field. There is no eye pain.
distractor_notes: Acute angle-closure glaucoma causes severe ocular pain, redness, headache, and often nausea with a fixed mid-dilated pupil.
Central retinal artery occlusion causes sudden profound painless vision loss but not typically preceding flashes, floaters, and a curtain-like field defect.
Optic neuritis commonly causes painful eye movement and central visual loss, often in younger adults.
Cataract causes slowly progressive painless blurring rather than sudden flashes, floaters, and a field curtain.
key_expl: Sudden photopsias, new floaters, and a painless curtain-like field defect are classic for retinal detachment.
objective: Recognize retinal detachment from sudden flashes, floaters, and a curtain-like visual-field loss.

sources.title: Retinal Detachment
sources.support: NEI describes flashes, floaters, and a curtain or shadow in the field of vision as warning symptoms of retinal detachment.

sources.title: Retinal detachment
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes retinal detachment as separation of the retina causing flashes, floaters, and visual-field loss.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Loss of the NF2 tumor suppressor merlin permits excessive proliferation of Schwann and other nervous-system support cells, predisposing especially to bilateral vestibular schwannomas.
vignette: A 21-year-old woman develops progressive bilateral hearing loss and imbalance. MRI shows tumors at both cerebellopontine angles involving the vestibular nerves.
lead: Loss of which protein most likely underlies this disorder?
distractor_notes: Neurofibromin is the NF1 tumor suppressor and its loss causes neurofibromatosis type 1.
Menin is the MEN1 tumor suppressor involved in multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1.
Tuberin is encoded by TSC2 and participates in tuberous sclerosis complex.
Fibrillin-1 is an extracellular matrix protein affected in Marfan syndrome.
key_expl: NF2 encodes merlin, a tumor suppressor; biallelic loss in susceptible cells predisposes to bilateral vestibular schwannomas.
objective: Associate bilateral vestibular schwannomas with loss of the NF2-encoded tumor suppressor merlin.
clues: young adult with progressive hearing loss

sources.title: Neurofibromatosis type 2
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes NF2 as a tumor-predisposition disorder characterized by bilateral vestibular schwannomas.

sources.title: NF2 gene
sources.support: NF2 encodes merlin, a tumor suppressor that helps regulate cell growth and adhesion.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: GAA-repeat expansion in FXN reduces frataxin, impairing mitochondrial iron handling and oxidative metabolism and causing progressive neurologic and cardiac injury.
vignette: A 15-year-old girl has progressive gait ataxia, absent lower-extremity reflexes, loss of vibration sense, scoliosis, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
lead: The deficient protein in this disorder is particularly important for normal function of which organelle?
distractor_notes: Lysosomal enzyme deficiencies cause storage disorders but do not explain the classic Friedreich phenotype.
Golgi dysfunction is not the primary cellular defect in Friedreich ataxia.
Peroxisomal dysfunction causes disorders such as X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy, not Friedreich ataxia.
Rough endoplasmic reticulum dysfunction is not the key organellar mechanism of frataxin deficiency.
key_expl: Frataxin is a mitochondrial protein; deficiency impairs mitochondrial function and iron-sulfur biology in energy-demanding tissues.
objective: Connect Friedreich ataxia to frataxin deficiency and mitochondrial dysfunction.
clues: ataxia with absent reflexes and sensory loss

sources.title: Friedreich ataxia
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes Friedreich ataxia as an FXN-related disorder affecting nervous and cardiac tissues.

sources.title: FXN gene
sources.support: FXN encodes frataxin, a mitochondrial protein involved in iron-sulfur cluster biology and mitochondrial function.
